output:
*Interview with Bastien Girard, établisseur, in the dining room. Second interview of the night.*

MATTHEY: Monsieur Girard, I am sorry to keep you up. Aurèle Monnier is dead, and I must ask everyone in the house the same questions. You are a guest here, not one of the family, so I will begin with how you came to be at the house.

GIRARD: I came as I come every year, Inspector. Aurèle asks the trade to dinner at the end of the year so he can look at our watches and tell us what is wrong with them. He never sent me home without a list of my own mistakes.

MATTHEY: You have known him a long time?

GIRARD: Twenty years. I buy movements and parts from men like him, I assemble them, and I sell the watch under my own name from Le Locle. A merchant learns a man by how he haggles. Aurèle did not haggle. He named his price and waited for you to sulk.

MATTHEY: Tell me about the repeater.

GIRARD: Four years he has worked on that piece. It is the best thing in his atelier and he knows it. I offered him money for the rights to make it under my name, and he told me I could not afford his opinion, let alone his watch. We quarrelled over the price at table. I said he was a robber of his own craft. He laughed and said I was a robber of other men's. Then he went back to his plate.

MATTHEY: Was anyone else involved in that discussion?

GIRARD: Félix, a little. He wants his uncle to be pleased with him, and his uncle is never pleased. Félix also owes me money, Inspector. Not a great deal, but enough that I notice when he laughs. He laughs when he is frightened.

MATTHEY: And Dr Vauthier?

GIRARD: Vauthier was there with his cigars and his Latin. I do not care for his company. He talks as though the rest of us were patients waiting for his opinion.

MATTHEY: Please tell me what you did after dinner.

GIRARD: When the temple struck ten, my watch showed four minutes to ten. I sat on alone in the dining room with the brandy. I did not want more talk.

MATTHEY: Where did you go then?

GIRARD: Into the street. I smoke Brissago when I have nothing better, and I had nothing better. It was a hard frost, and the snow in the road was old and grey. I went out into the street to smoke at twenty-one minutes past ten by my watch, and I stayed under the front windows of the house. I walk in the cold when I want to think. I wanted to think about the price of his repeater.

MATTHEY: What did you hear from the street?

GIRARD: The piano started up in the salon just as I lit my cigar, at twenty-nine minutes past ten by my watch. It stopped at eighteen minutes to eleven by my watch.

MATTHEY: Did you hear anything else while the piano was playing?

GIRARD: At twenty-six minutes to eleven by my watch I heard faint quick bells from the master's window up above, and the piano was playing all the while. I know a repeater's voice. The low notes are the hours, the doubled note is the quarter, and the high quick notes are the minutes past it. That was a repeater, and it was at the top of the house.

MATTHEY: Then what did you do?

GIRARD: I came back into the house at fourteen minutes to eleven by my watch. The hall clock had just struck eleven, and its face showed two minutes past eleven. I went up to Félix in the library.

MATTHEY: You looked at the hall clock?

GIRARD: I am a merchant, Inspector. A merchant notices time. It is the first thing I look at when I come into a house and the last thing I look at when I leave one.

MATTHEY: Thank you, Monsieur Girard. Please remain in the house until I have finished with the others.
